annotations.description:
Largest Contentful Paint at the 50th percentile. A median above 2.5s means the site is broadly slow rather than slow for a segment: suspect something that changed for everyone, most often image weight above the fold or a new render-blocking script.

MEASURED BASELINE, 2026-09-05, 24h: p50 is 0.87s, so this rule has roughly 3x headroom and only fires on a severe, site-wide regression. That is deliberate - p75 is the rule that tracks the standard, and this one exists to say 'everyone, not a segment'. See the p75 rule for the full baseline and the sub-part breakdown queries.

STREAM SELECTOR: `kind` is NOT a Loki label - it must be parsed with `| logfmt | kind="measurement"`. Selecting it as a label matches nothing and, with No Data: OK, reads as a fast site. This whole group shipped that way and was blind for two days.

WINDOW AND SAMPLE FLOOR: about 32 LCP samples an hour, so the window is 6h (roughly 190 samples) and the floor 100. The original 1h window could not support a percentile at all.

DATA PATH: the Faro Web SDK is bundled into the server's JavaScript and posts to https://tuist.dev/-/faro/collect, routed to the Alloy faro.receiver. The logfmt line carries lcp in MILLISECONDS, hence the /1000. app_environment is "prod", not "production".

annotations.description:
Largest Contentful Paint at the 99th percentile over 24h. Fires only when p99 > 10s, there are more than 300 LCP samples, and at least 10 distinct sessions have an LCP > 10s, sustained for 30 minutes. This finds a severe tail affecting multiple sessions; the p75 rule measures typical site performance against the Core Web Vitals threshold.

A = p99 in seconds. B = total LCP samples. D = distinct non-empty session_id values with lcp > 10000 milliseconds in the same 24h window. Repeated loads in one session count once. C = $A > 10.0 && $B > 300 && $D >= 10. D returns a labeled zero when LCP telemetry exists but no sessions qualify; missing telemetry is covered by the separate browser-vitals telemetry rule.

AFFECTED-SESSION FLOOR ADDED 2026-09-06: the investigated September 5 21:46 UTC window had p99 13.58s across 477 samples, but only six affected sessions on different pages. A 14-day lookback returned only about 54 hours of LCP history. Of 55 hourly evaluation points, the old condition crossed its thresholds at 19; all had fewer than 10 affected sessions (maximum 8). Ten is an interruption policy, not a statistically established cutoff. Reassess with more history; this can delay detection on low-traffic pages. The lower-percentile rules remain independent.

Go to the per-page breakdown, and check sample counts alongside percentiles:
topk(10, quantile_over_time(0.99, {service_name="tuist-web"} | logfmt | kind="measurement" | type="web-vitals" | app_environment="prod" | lcp!="" | unwrap lcp [24h]) by (page_url)) / 1000

Check mise run marketing:image-budget first, but it only covers static/marketing/images (500 KB per static image, 3.2 MB per GIF). App assets such as the signup images are outside that budget. Inspect context_element and resource_load_duration. A long TTFB does not prove a slow origin: correlate context_navigation_entry_id with event_data_faroNavigationId on faro.performance.navigation and inspect DNS, connection, TLS and request timings. One September 5 blog visit spent 35.51s establishing its connection and 0.57s loading the LCP image.

The 10s threshold is unchanged. The earlier measured p99 baseline was 7.11s; p75 has its own rule. kind is NOT an indexed Loki label: parse it with | logfmt | kind="measurement". app_environment is prod and LCP values are milliseconds.

annotations.description:
THIS RULE IS THE SAFETY NET FOR THE WHOLE 'Web performance' GROUP. The LCP percentile rules (p50, p75, p90, p95, p99) are threshold rules with No Data: OK, so a collector that stops receiving looks exactly like a fast site. Without this rule, breaking the Faro pipeline silences all of them permanently and reads as health.

NOTE THE INVERTED POLARITY, the opposite of the rules it guards: No Data is Alerting here, not OK. An empty result is the failure being detected - if the stream disappears entirely, sum(count_over_time(...)) returns nothing rather than zero, so a threshold alone would never fire.

EXPECTED VOLUME: about 32 LCP samples an hour, so a healthy 2h window holds roughly 60. The threshold is <1, i.e. total silence, not a volume dip.

THIS PIPELINE HAS SHIPPED THREE SILENT FAULTS. All three looked identical from the alert list - every rule green - so check them before anything else:

  (a) PATH. Alloy's faro.receiver serves POST on /collect alone. Payloads got a plain-text '404 page not found' from Alloy's router until the collector URL was moved to /-/faro/collect.

  (b) ENVIRONMENT SPELLING. The app emits app_environment="prod" (Tuist.Environment.env(), same as Sentry). The rules filtered "production", the k8s label spelling, and matched nothing.

  (c) KIND AS A LABEL. Alloy's exporter sets kind as a stream label, but Grafana Cloud does not index it - the only stream labels are cluster, env, k8s_cluster_name, service_name, detected_level. Selecting {service_name="tuist-web", kind="measurement"} matches nothing; kind must be parsed with | logfmt | kind="measurement". This one hid two days of perfectly good data.

The shape of all three is the same: a filter that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a fast site when No Data is OK. When in doubt, strip the pipeline back to {service_name="tuist-web"} and add stages one at a time.

WHERE TO LOOK, in the order the payload travels:

  1. The browser - view source on tuist.dev and confirm globalThis.analytics has a collector_url. Empty means TUIST_FARO_COLLECTOR_URL is unset (server.faro.collectorUrl in the tuist chart).

  2. The ingress - curl -sX POST https://tuist.dev/-/faro/collect -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}' should return 202. READ THE BODY OF ANY 404: a plain-text '404 page not found' is Go's, so the request reached Alloy and the path is wrong. An HTML error page means it never left Phoenix, so the Faro Ingress or ExternalName Service was not rendered.

  3. Loki - strip the query to {service_name="tuist-web"} and check raw volume, then re-add | logfmt | kind="measurement" and each filter in turn.

  4. Alloy - faro_receiver_measurements_total on the alloy-receiver collector counts what it ingested. Rising there but absent in Loki is a forwarding problem. Absent entirely proves nothing on its own: those component metrics are not always exported to Grafana Cloud.

  5. Content blockers cannot explain a total outage: the collector is same-origin on tuist.dev precisely so no blocklist matches it.

annotations.description:
THIS IS THE ONE RULE IN THE GROUP THAT MEASURES A STANDARD RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. Core Web Vitals assesses LCP at the 75th percentile: at or below 2.5s is good, above 4.0s is poor. p75 is what CrUX publishes and what Google Search's page-experience signal reads, so it is the number an outside party quotes when they say tuist.dev is slow. The p50/p90/p95/p99 rules describe the SHAPE of a regression; only this one answers whether we are passing.

MEASURED BASELINE, 2026-09-05, 24h, 768 LCP samples: p50 0.87s, p75 1.57s, p90 2.87s, p95 3.81s, p99 7.11s. Ratings: 88% good, 8% needs-improvement, 4% poor. So p75 sits at 1.57s against a 2.5s bar - passing comfortably, and inside the 1.2-1.8s target for a mostly static site behind Cloudflare with TTFB around 117ms. Firing means roughly a 60% regression, not a marginal drift.

STREAM SELECTOR: `kind` is NOT a Loki label here. Alloy's exporter sets it, but Grafana Cloud does not index it - the only stream labels are cluster, env, k8s_cluster_name, service_name and detected_level. It has to be parsed out of the line with `| logfmt | kind="measurement"`. Selecting `{service_name="tuist-web", kind="measurement"}` matches nothing, and with No Data: OK that reads as a fast site. Every rule in this group shipped that way and was blind for two days.

WHERE THE TIME WENT. Google's LCP sub-part budget is TTFB at most 40% of LCP, resource load delay at most 10%, resource load duration at most 40%, element render delay at most 10%. Faro records all four next to the value:

  quantile_over_time(0.75, {service_name="tuist-web"} | logfmt | kind="measurement" | type="web-vitals" | lcp!="" | unwrap resource_load_duration [6h]) by (app_environment)

Swap in time_to_first_byte, resource_load_delay or element_render_delay. Large resource_load_duration is image weight; large time_to_first_byte is the origin.

WINDOW AND SAMPLE FLOOR: traffic is about 32 LCP samples an hour, so a 1h window cannot support a percentile at all - 6h gives roughly 190. The B floor of 100 is set from that measured rate, not guessed.

Core Web Vitals is officially assessed over 28 days. 6h is an operational proxy that catches a regression the same day; do not read a passing 6h window as a passing CrUX assessment, which covers Chrome users only.

annotations.description:
Clients are waiting on the remote compilation cache. This is measured from what Xcode recorded per task (default.cacheable_tasks.read_duration for status hit_remote, CI builds from default.build_runs), not from server metrics. Kura's own latency stays low when the delay is added between the client and Kura, which is what happened on 2026-09-14/15: Kura p90 stayed under 3.5 ms while clients read at 230 ms and more for 20-30 minute stretches of their builds.

Fires when, for CI builds ingested in the last hour: at least 1000 remote reads over at least 3 builds, at least 2 builds with read p90 above 200 ms, more than 10% of reads above 150 ms, and that share at least 4x the account's own share over the previous 7 days (1-in-20 build sample, at least 1000 reads). The comparison against the account's own history is deliberate: some accounts read slowly all the time (clients far from their region, or a heavy tail), and an absolute threshold fires on them every day.

Known causes:
1. The regional Kura ingress returned malformed responses (status 009 or HTTP/2 000, gRPC 502) because nginx reused upstream connections across gRPC and HTTP. Check 'Kura - ingress returning malformed or 502 responses' for the account's instances.
2. The CLI's CAS proxy re-resolves its endpoint every 10 minutes with one latency probe per region, and a single failed probe moves it to another region for at least 10 minutes. Those builds show a stretch where even p10 read latency sits at the far region's round trip (220 ms and more), then an abrupt return.

Find the builds (Grafana Explore, tuist-production-clickhouse, replace ACCOUNT):
SELECT br.id, br.ins, round(br.dur / 60000, 1) AS minutes, count() AS reads, round(quantile(0.1)(ct.read_duration)) AS p10, round(quantile(0.5)(ct.read_duration)) AS p50, round(quantile(0.9)(ct.read_duration)) AS p90 FROM cacheable_tasks AS ct INNER JOIN (SELECT id, any(inserted_at) AS ins, any(duration) AS dur FROM build_runs WHERE account_id = ACCOUNT AND is_ci AND inserted_at >= now() - INTERVAL 6 HOUR GROUP BY id) AS br ON br.id = ct.build_run_id WHERE ct.build_run_id IN (SELECT id FROM build_runs WHERE account_id = ACCOUNT AND is_ci AND inserted_at >= now() - INTERVAL 6 HOUR) AND ct.status = 'hit_remote' AND ct.read_duration > 0 GROUP BY br.id, br.ins, minutes ORDER BY br.ins
A slow build reads at hundreds of ms at p90 while the account's other builds read at tens. Do not alias an aggregate with the name of a column the same query filters on (any(account_id) AS account_id): ClickHouse resolves the WHERE to the alias and rejects the query.

Write latency is not part of the condition: normal per-build write p90 ranges from 30 ms to several seconds depending on upload size, so it cannot separate an incident from a large upload.

Limits: only processed builds count, so the rule lags a slow build by its duration plus processing. Hits replayed from the local CAS never reach cacheable_tasks. Each evaluation reads about 130M rows (3 GiB, 4 s); the group runs every 10 minutes.

Background: infra/helm/k8s-monitoring/alerts.md, section 'CI remote compilation-cache reads slow for an account'.
annotations.summary: Account {{ $labels.account_id }}: {{ $values.A.Value | humanizePercentage }} of CI remote compilation-cache reads took over 150 ms in the last hour

model.rawSql:
WITH
recent AS (
  SELECT id, any(account_id) AS acct FROM build_runs
  WHERE inserted_at >= now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR AND is_ci
  GROUP BY id
),
base AS (
  SELECT id, any(account_id) AS acct FROM build_runs
  WHERE inserted_at >= now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND inserted_at < now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR AND is_ci
    AND cityHash64(id) % 20 = 0 AND account_id IN (SELECT acct FROM recent)
  GROUP BY id
),
recent_builds AS (
  SELECT r.acct AS acct, ct.build_run_id AS build, count() AS reads,
    countIf(ct.read_duration > 150) AS slow_reads, quantile(0.9)(ct.read_duration) AS p90
  FROM cacheable_tasks AS ct INNER JOIN recent AS r ON r.id = ct.build_run_id
  WHERE ct.build_run_id IN (SELECT id FROM recent) AND ct.status = 'hit_remote' AND ct.read_duration > 0
  GROUP BY acct, build
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT b.acct AS acct, count() AS base_reads, countIf(ct.read_duration > 150) / count() AS base_share
  FROM cacheable_tasks AS ct INNER JOIN base AS b ON b.id = ct.build_run_id
  WHERE ct.build_run_id IN (SELECT id FROM base) AND ct.status = 'hit_remote' AND ct.read_duration > 0
  GROUP BY acct
)
SELECT toString(rb.acct) AS account_id,
  round(sum(rb.slow_reads) / sum(rb.reads), 3) AS slow_read_share
FROM recent_builds AS rb INNER JOIN baseline AS bl ON bl.acct = rb.acct
GROUP BY account_id
HAVING sum(rb.reads) >= 1000
  AND count() >= 3
  AND countIf(rb.p90 > 200 AND rb.reads >= 100) >= 2
  AND slow_read_share >= 0.1
  AND any(bl.base_reads) >= 1000
  AND slow_read_share >= 4 * any(bl.base_share)

annotations.description:
The {{ $labels.device }} filesystem on bare-metal node {{ $labels.instance }} ({{ $labels.env }}) has been above 80% for 15 minutes (currently {{ $values.A.Value | humanizePercentage }}).

Why this matters: these boxes back the Kura CAS ring and runner caches through local-path volumes, where the PVC's declared size bounds nothing. The ring is budgeted from KURA_CAS_CAPACITY_BYTES rather than enforced by the volume, so nothing stops the box itself from filling. kubelet on this fleet runs eviction-hard imagefs.available<15% (infra/k8s/clusters/bare-metal.yaml), so it starts evicting at 85% used, and it will evict the region's pods before Kura's ring rotation gets a chance to evict segments. That ordering is what took eu-central down.

80% is roughly four accounts' envelopes on a ~846GiB Kura box; the fifth would land past the eviction threshold. The fix is a second box, not a bigger budget.

Likely causes:
- An account provisioned onto a box already near its envelope ceiling
- A region's disk_envelope_size raised beyond what the box can hold
- Upload staging (KURA_TMP_DIR, 8GiB per replica) or the RocksDB index growing past its reserve
- Non-Kura growth on the same disk: container images, logs, or a runner cache

Note the disks differ by fleet: kura and ovh boxes keep the ring on /, while dedibox boxes keep it on a separate device mounted at /opt/local-path-provisioner (their / is only ~19GiB).

Dashboard: /d/tuist-kura

annotations.description:
Tailscale operator proxy {{ $labels.proxy }} on {{ $labels.cluster }} has had zero ready replicas for 30 minutes, so the tailnet path it carries is down.

What the proxies carry: every StatefulSet in the tailscale-operator namespace is a proxy the operator runs. ts-tuist-cluster-subnet-router-* is the Connector subnet router, the path from the Mac minis to in-cluster Services such as Kura. macmini-egress is the egress ProxyGroup alloy-metrics uses to scrape the Mac minis. The other ts-* proxies each expose one Service to the tailnet (Postgres pooler, ClickHouse, the Alloy receiver, tuist-ops).

Why the rule keys on the proxy and not the StatefulSet: the Connector, ProxyClass and ProxyGroup are Helm post-upgrade hooks with before-hook-creation, so every tailscale-operator deploy recreates the Connector StatefulSet under a new generated suffix. The query strips that suffix so the pending period survives a redeploy. From 2026-06-18 to 2026-09-23 the staging subnet router sat Pending, because its ProxyClass pinned it to the tainted kura-scw-fr-par pool without a toleration. It was replaced up to 25 times a day, so no single Pod or StatefulSet ever looked stuck, and nothing fired.

What to do: kubectl -n tailscale-operator get statefulsets,pods, then describe the proxy Pod.
- Pending: read the FailedScheduling event. The nodeSelector and tolerations come from the ProxyClass in infra/helm/tailscale-operator.
- Running but not Ready: kubectl logs <pod> -c tailscale. Usually an auth key, tag or ACL problem.
- For the Connector, confirm the routes with kubectl exec <pod> -c tailscale -- tailscale status --json and read .Self.PrimaryRoutes.

This can leave zero backends to serve traffic, causing user-facing 503s (seen previously during node/egress failures and readiness-probe flapping). Set the alert's pending duration (For) to 2-5m to avoid flapping on brief rollout blips.
annotations.summary: tuist-tuist-server has fewer available replicas ({{ $values.A }}) than desired ({{ $values.B }}) in tuist-production.

model.expr: kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{deployment="tuist-tuist-server", namespace="tuist", cluster="tuist-production"}
kube_deployment_spec_replicas{deployment="tuist-tuist-server", namespace="tuist", cluster="tuist-production"}

rules.title: Tuist Server - Available Replicas Below Spec

annotations.description:
At least one etcd member across the CAPI fleet reports no leader for 2 minutes. While a member has no leader it serves no writes, and if a quorum is affected the cluster's API server is read-only: deploys, scaling and CAPI reconciliation all stall.

Reading the value: it is the COUNT of etcd members currently without a leader, not a cluster name. These series are subject to Grafana Cloud adaptive metrics, which aggregates away cluster, env, instance and k8s_cluster_name - so this rule cannot say which cluster or which member. Identify the member by hand from the management cluster.

Why it is written as count minus sum rather than the obvious min(...) == 0: adaptive metrics only serves the aggregations it stores for a metric, which here are sum and count. min by (cluster, instance) (etcd_server_has_leader) == bool 0 returns NO DATA, not 0 - so the rule that reads most naturally is silently dead, and with noDataState OK it can never fire. etcd_server_has_leader is a 0/1 gauge, so count minus sum is exactly the number of members without a leader and is equivalent to min == 0. Before changing this expression, run it and confirm it returns a series.
annotations.summary: An etcd member has lost its leader

model.expr: count by (cluster) (etcd_server_has_leader) - sum by (cluster) (etcd_server_has_leader)

annotations.description:
Across the CAPI fleet, desired KubeadmControlPlane replicas exceed ready replicas for 15 minutes. A control plane short a replica has lost redundancy; short two of three has lost etcd quorum and its API server is read-only.

Reading the value: it is the fleet-wide COUNT of missing control-plane replicas, not a cluster name. These series are subject to Grafana Cloud adaptive metrics, which aggregates away the kubeadmcontrolplane and workload_cluster labels, so the sums are over every workload cluster and this rule cannot say which one is degraded. Get that from the management cluster with kubectl get kubeadmcontrolplane -A. The 15 minute window is deliberately longer than a rolling control-plane replacement, which briefly shows the same shortfall.

When healthy this evaluates to an explicit 0 rather than an empty result, so No Data here means the telemetry itself stopped rather than that the fleet is well - which is what the paired telemetry-missing rule alerts on.
annotations.summary: A CAPI control plane has fewer ready replicas than desired

model.expr: sum by (cluster) (kube_customresource_kubeadmcontrolplane_spec_replicas) - sum by (cluster) (kube_customresource_kubeadmcontrolplane_ready_replicas)

rules.title: CAPI - control plane below desired replicas

annotations.description:
No KubeadmControlPlane series have arrived from the management cluster for 15 minutes.

Why this rule exists: this is the heartbeat that stops the monitor failing silent with the thing it monitors. Every other CAPI rule reads series produced by kube-state-metrics on the single-node management cluster. If that cluster, its Alloy collector, or its remote-write path dies, all of those rules simply stop having data and go quiet - which looks identical to healthy. Evaluation runs in Grafana Cloud, outside the cluster being watched, so it still fires when the cluster is gone.

Two query details that are easy to get wrong here, both of which produced a false alert while this rule was being written:
- These series are subject to Grafana Cloud adaptive metrics, which aggregates away the kubeadmcontrolplane and workload_cluster labels. The raw series cannot be selected at all, so this aggregates with sum by (cluster); selecting the raw metric reports absent even while data flows.
- absent() returns an EMPTY result when the data is present, which Grafana evaluates as NoData. noDataState must therefore be OK, not Alerting: the healthy case is no data from absent(), and the firing case is absent() returning 1. Setting noDataState to Alerting inverts the rule and it fires permanently.

What to do: check the management cluster is reachable, then kube-state-metrics and the alloy-metrics collector in its observability namespace. Until this clears, treat every other CAPI alert as unverified rather than passing - none of them can fire.
annotations.summary: CAPI control-plane telemetry has stopped arriving from the management cluster

model.expr: absent(sum by (cluster) (kube_customresource_kubeadmcontrolplane_spec_replicas))

rules.title: CAPI - control-plane telemetry missing from the management cluster

annotations.description:
A server exists in the Hetzner Cloud project that no CAPI Machine claims: billed, running, and tracked by neither git nor CAPI.

Why this matters: this is one of the three failures behind spec/72. Two orphaned worker VMs billed for weeks with no owning Cluster; neither git nor CAPI reflected them, so no reconciler could ever have noticed. Cost is the mild consequence; the real one is an unmanaged machine with cluster credentials still attached.

The check runs every 30 minutes from the reconciliation-checks CronJob on the management cluster. This cluster's own nodes are excluded (mgmt does not self-manage, so its VM legitimately has no Machine), which is why a healthy result is exactly zero rather than one.

What to do: identify the server by the id and name in this alert. If it is a leftover from a deleted Cluster, delete it in Hetzner. If it is something deliberately provisioned outside CAPI, it needs to become a Node of this cluster or be added to the exclusion in reconciliation-checks.yaml, otherwise this fires forever and gets ignored.
annotations.summary: Hetzner server {{ $labels.name }} (id {{ $labels.id }}) has no owning CAPI Machine

model.expr: max by (cluster, id, name) (capi_reconciliation_orphan_server{cluster="tuist-management"})

rules.title: CAPI - orphan Hetzner server with no owning Machine

annotations.description:
A Cluster that Flux has managed is no longer in any Flux Kustomization inventory: it was removed from git, but the infrastructure is still running.

Why this matters: the Flux Kustomizations are deliberately configured prune: false, so deleting a manifest from git never tears down a live cluster. That is the right default (a bad merge cannot destroy production), but it leaves a blind spot: the cluster keeps running, keeps billing, and nothing in git describes it any more. The Hetzner orphan check cannot see it either, because its servers still have valid Machine owners.

Membership is derived from the kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/name label, so Clusters managed outside Flux by mgmt-cluster-apply.yml (preview, pentest) are never counted and no exclusion list has to be maintained.

What to do: decide whether the removal was intentional. If it was, complete the explicit destroy flow: kubectl delete cluster under break-glass (see infra/flux/mgmt/README.md). If it was not, restore the manifest - the cluster has been running unmanaged since the removal.
annotations.summary: Cluster {{ $labels.name }} is live but no longer present in git

model.expr: max by (cluster, name) (capi_reconciliation_stale_cluster{cluster="tuist-management"})

rules.title: CAPI - Cluster removed from git but still running

annotations.description:
The reconciliation-checks CronJob on the management cluster has not recorded a successful completion for over 90 minutes. While it is stopped, the orphan-Hetzner-server and stale-cluster alerts cannot fire: they read gauges this job pushes, so they go quiet rather than green.

Threshold is 5400s, three times the 30 minute schedule, so a single missed run does not page.

Why the age of a timestamp rather than absent(): the job pushes to a Pushgateway, which is a store and not a scrape target. Once a value is pushed it is served indefinitely, so the gauges never disappear on their own and absent() over them can never fire no matter how long the job has been dead. The completion stamp is what makes a stopped job detectable at all.

no_data_state is OK per the house convention. The case this rule cannot see - the Pushgateway losing its store entirely, so there is no timestamp to age - is covered by the paired rule CAPI - reconciliation telemetry absent entirely. Do not delete that rule without changing this one.

What to do: check the CronJob and its recent Jobs in the org-tuist namespace on the management cluster.
annotations.summary: Orphan-server and stale-cluster checks have stopped completing

model.expr: time() - max by (cluster) (capi_reconciliation_last_success_timestamp_seconds{cluster="tuist-management"})

rules.title: CAPI - reconciliation checks have stopped running

annotations.description:
No reconciliation-check completion stamp has been seen for a full hour. This is the blind spot of the paired rule CAPI - reconciliation checks have stopped running: that one alerts on the AGE of the completion timestamp, which requires the timestamp to exist. If the Pushgateway loses its store, or was never scraped, there is no series to age and that rule goes quiet instead of firing.

The Pushgateway store is deliberately ephemeral: there is no persistence file, because it would sit on an emptyDir and be wiped on restart anyway. After a bounce the gauges are simply absent until the next run, at most 30 minutes later, which is well inside this one hour window - so a restart plus one missed run does not page.

no_data_state is OK, per the house convention: absent_over_time returns a series only when the metric is gone, so an empty result is the healthy state. Alerting here would invert the rule.

What to do: check the reconciliation-pushgateway Deployment in the observability namespace and that alloy-metrics is still scraping it via its prometheus.io/scrape pod annotation.
annotations.summary: Reconciliation-check telemetry is absent entirely (Pushgateway reset or never scraped)

model.expr: absent_over_time(capi_reconciliation_last_success_timestamp_seconds{cluster="tuist-management"}[1h])

annotations.description:
No Flux controller on the management cluster has completed a single reconciliation in an hour. Normal is roughly 120 per hour across the seven Kustomizations and the GitRepository.

Why this matters: Flux is what keeps the workload Cluster resources matching git. A stalled reconciler does not break anything immediately, it silently stops correcting drift, so the fleet quietly diverges from the repository and the next real change never lands. Nothing else notices.

This is a fleet TOTAL on purpose. Suspending one Kustomization is a normal operation (see the suspend and resume section in infra/flux/mgmt/README.md) and must not page, so this fires only when all reconciliation has stopped: source-controller cannot reach git, kustomize-controller is crash-looping or wedged, or the controllers are gone.

It does not detect a reconcile that runs and FAILS, because the duration histogram counts failures too. That is the paired rule Flux - Kustomization is not Ready.

What to do: check the flux-system namespace on the management cluster, then the GitRepository's Ready condition and artifact revision.
annotations.summary: Flux has not completed any reconciliation in the last hour

model.expr: sum(increase(gotk_reconcile_duration_seconds_count{cluster="tuist-management"}[1h]))

annotations.description:
No gotk_reconcile_duration_seconds_count series has arrived for 30 minutes.

This is the paired absent rule for Flux - reconciliation has stalled fleet-wide. That rule compares a counter against a threshold, so if the Flux controllers disappear entirely the series goes away, the comparison returns No Data, and per the house convention No Data renders as Normal. In other words the stall rule cannot see the most severe case: Flux not running at all. This rule can.

Causes to check in order: the Flux controller pods are gone or crash-looping in flux-system, the alloy-metrics collector on the management cluster is down, or the pod-annotation scrape that picks these up has stopped matching. Note the Flux metrics are collected by annotation autodiscovery rather than by an explicit scrape config, so a change to those annotations silently stops collection.

While this is firing, treat Flux - reconciliation has stalled fleet-wide as unverified rather than passing.
annotations.summary: Flux controller telemetry has stopped arriving from the management cluster

model.expr: absent_over_time(gotk_reconcile_duration_seconds_count{cluster="tuist-management"}[30m])

rules.title: Flux - telemetry missing from the management cluster

annotations.description:
Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} on {{ $labels.cluster }} has been unschedulable for 30 minutes: the scheduler has a Pod it cannot place on any node.

Why this matters: an unscheduled Pod produces none of the signals the other workload rules read. It has no container, so there is no waiting reason, no termination reason and no restart count, and it never had a ready endpoint to lose. Its Services keep existing with zero endpoints, which reads as 'no traffic' rather than 'no backend'. That is how registry/registry-pg-1, the sole instance of a CloudNativePG cluster, sat Pending in production from 2026-07-06 to 2026-08-19 with all three of its Services on zero endpoints and nobody noticing. The series backing this rule existed in Grafana Cloud for that entire window; nothing read it.

Likely causes:
- A PersistentVolume whose node affinity no surviving node satisfies. Hetzner Cloud Volumes are location-bound, so a volume provisioned against a node that was later destroyed strands its Pod permanently. Compare the PVC's volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node annotation against the current node list, and check the volume's location.
- Untolerated taints after a node-pool change, or a nodeSelector naming a pool that no longer exists.
- Genuine capacity: no node has room for the Pod's resource requests.

What to do: kubectl describe pod and read the FailedScheduling event. It reports a count per reason (untolerated taint, PersistentVolume node affinity, insufficient resources) across all nodes, which normally identifies the cause without further digging.

Scope note: this rule is deliberately limited to tuist-production. tuist-staging currently carries around 15 permanently unschedulable Pods (14 in kura, largely scaled-to-zero dev meshes, plus tailscale-operator subnet-router churn), so extending it there would fire continuously until those are cleaned up. tuist-runners is excluded for a different reason: the autoscaler deliberately over-asks and the surplus sits unschedulable by design, and queue age already covers the real failure there.

Dashboard: /d/tuist-kura
annotations.summary: Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} has been unschedulable for 30 minutes in {{ $labels.cluster }}

model.expr: max by (cluster, namespace, pod) (kube_pod_status_unschedulable{cluster="tuist-production", namespace!="tuist-runners"}) == 1

annotations.description:
The oldest queued workflow job on {{ $labels.fleet }} that its account has the concurrency headroom to run has been waiting over 30 minutes (currently {{ $values.A.Value | humanizeDuration }}). Healthy waits are seconds, and the worst legitimate burst observed is a few minutes.

Why this matters: Tuist runners do not use GitHub's native queue. The server ingests workflow_job webhooks into Postgres runner_workflow_jobs, the autoscaler sizes each pool from that queue, and polling Pods claim work through the dispatch endpoint. So a job can sit queued on GitHub indefinitely while runner Pods sit idle in a *different* pool — GitHub reports no error, and before this alert nothing else noticed. On 2026-07-16 a tuist-macos job sat queued for 4h08m exactly this way and silently stalled the production deploy cascade, which gates on needs.acceptance-tests.result == 'success'.

This measures DISPATCHABLE age. Queued work whose account is at its concurrency limit is excluded, because dispatch declines it and the autoscaler declines to grow the fleet for it, both on purpose. Otherwise it still fires on age alone: conditioning on idle capacity would have missed the very incident it was written for.

Likely causes:
- The pool has no host slots because a sibling pool is holding them → compare tuist_runners_autoscaler_allocated_replicas across pools sharing the fleet, and check ..._warm_deficit_replicas. Idle runners in another pool is the signature of a floor on the wrong pool, not a capacity shortfall.
- Pods scheduled but never booting — tart-kubelet stalled mid `tart pull`, common right after an image roll or on a fresh host with a cold image cache → Pods Pending with PodScheduled=True and no VM.
- The pool's minWarmPoolFloor is 0 and the p95 signal has decayed, so an off-peak arrival pays a full cold start.
- Dispatch erroring rather than starving → tuist_runners_dispatch_request_count by outcome.
- An account with NO runner_concurrency_limits row for the platform. Claims.attempt/5 fails that as :concurrency_limit_missing, so none of its jobs can ever be claimed. Deliberately NOT excluded from this measurement — a broken invariant is a fault, not a cap — so it reaches you here rather than reading as a healthy zero.

Not this: an account parked at its concurrency limit. That work is excluded from this measurement by design. Confirm with tuist_runners_queue_withheld against tuist_runners_queue_length on /d/tuist-runners, and treat a sustained gap as an entitlement question — their limit versus what they bought — rather than an incident. The limit is a resource budget per account and platform, shared across every shape on it.

Not this: a dropped webhook. Nothing would be queued server-side, so this gauge would read 0 and the alert would stay silent — that gap is covered by WebhookRedeliveryWorker.

Note: the query carries a transitional `or` fallback to tuist_runners_queue_oldest_age_seconds so coverage is continuous until tuist/tuist#12765 deploys. Drop the fallback once the new metric is reporting on every fleet.

Dashboard: /d/tuist-runners
Logs: {service_name="tuist-server"} |= "runners:"
annotations.summary: Runner fleet {{ $labels.fleet }} in {{ $labels.cluster }}: oldest dispatchable queued job waiting {{ $values.A.Value | humanizeDuration }}

model.expr: max by (cluster, env, fleet) (tuist_runners_queue_oldest_dispatchable_age_seconds{env="production"}) or max by (cluster, env, fleet) (tuist_runners_queue_oldest_age_seconds{env="production"})

annotations.description:
The root APFS volume on macOS runner host {{ $labels.instance }} ({{ $labels.env }}) has under 10% free for 15m (currently {{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.1f" }}%).

Why this matters: the host stores Tart golden base images (~68G each) on /; they accumulate (at ~6 goldens the 460GiB disk fills) and a full disk makes every operator SSH config update fail with 'No space left on device' while the Node still reports Ready. This is the fleet-wide fill that broke the runners fleet on 2026-07-20.

tart-kubelet now reclaims goldens at 15% free and reports DiskPressure below 10%; this alert is the backstop if reclaim can't keep up (e.g. every golden backs a live clone).

Likely causes:
- Golden GC not keeping up / disabled (--disable-vm-gc on a non-builder host is a bug)
- A burst of Xcode-version pools each pinning a golden on this host

What to do: SSH the host over the tailnet (Node InternalIP, user m1, key in Secret tuist-tuist-runners-fleet-ssh); `df -h /` and `du -shx ~/.tart/vms/tuist-golden-*`; delete the oldest stale goldens (APFS CoW keeps live clones intact). Root fix: golden retention/GC in tart-kubelet.
annotations.summary: Runner host {{ $labels.instance }} ({{ $labels.env }}) root disk {{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.1f" }}% free (< 10% buffer)

model.expr: min by (cluster, env, instance) (100 * node_filesystem_avail_bytes{job="tuist-macos-node-exporter", instance=~"tuist-tuist-runners-fleet-.*", mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{job="tuist-macos-node-exporter", instance=~"tuist-tuist-runners-fleet-.*", mountpoint="/"})

annotations.description:
ScalewayAppleSiliconMachine {{ $labels.machine }} in {{ $labels.cluster }} has been terminal Failed ({{ $labels.failure_reason }}) for 30m. The operator stops pushing config to a Failed machine, so it drifts on a stale tart-kubelet while its Node may still serve — otherwise only visible via `kubectl get machine`.

Most common cause is TartKubeletUpdateExceededRetries: the host SSH config update kept failing. READ THE OPERATOR LOG for the real error before clearing anything — it is usually one of:
- Full root disk ('No space left on device') -> free goldens on the host (see the Runner Host Disk Buffer alert / runbook), the clear alone won't help.
- Wedged sshd accept path ('dial :22 i/o timeout') -> transient; clearing the terminal state lets the operator retry.

Recover: once the underlying cause is fixed, clear the terminal state so the operator re-rolls: `kubectl -n tuist patch scalewayapplesiliconmachine {{ $labels.machine }} --subresource=status --type=merge -p '{"status":{"failureReason":null,"failureMessage":null,"failedHostConfigHash":null,"tartKubeletUpdateAttempts":0}}'` (break-glass; CAPI writes are not in the JIT edit tier). Also clear the sticky CAPI Machine phase if needed.
annotations.summary: Runner machine {{ $labels.machine }} ({{ $labels.cluster }}) stuck Failed: {{ $labels.failure_reason }}

model.expr: max by (cluster, machine, fleet, failure_reason) (capt_scaleway_applesilicon_machine_phase{phase="Failed", fleet="tuist-tuist-runners-fleet"})

annotations.description:
Cilium on the co-located runner-cache node {{ $labels.node }} has been dropping ingress packets as 'Policy denied' for 10m.

FIRST CHECK, before concluding anything: are the drops confined to ONE node? A runner VM talks to a single regional cache, so simultaneous drops across regions are never a mis-sourced host — they are a kura-controller rollout blip, and every merge to main rolls the controller. This rule is scoped node=~".*-kura-fleet-.*", so it shows you one node even when all four are dropping. Drop that matcher to see the truth:

  sum by (node) (rate(cilium_drop_count_total{direction="INGRESS", reason="Policy denied", cluster="$cluster"}[5m]) * on (cluster, pod) group_left(node) kube_pod_info{namespace="kube-system", pod=~"cilium-.*"}) > 0

These nodes do NOT sit at exactly zero. Two populations exist: transient bursts of 0.02-0.10 packets/s lasting a few minutes (controller rollouts, benign), and sustained episodes of 0.8-5 packets/s lasting 30 minutes to 6 hours (the real fault). The [5m] window plus the 10m pending period is what separates them, so the pending period means 'still dropping', not 'dropped recently'. Do not add a magnitude floor — it would hide a low-rate variant of the same fault.

Why a real one matters: the per-instance kura NetworkPolicy admits http only from namespaceSelector {} and ipBlock 172.16.0.0/22 (the Private Network). A macOS runner VM whose egress is not masqueraded to its host's PN VLAN address arrives from outside that block and is dropped at ingress silently, with no RST. The client never sees a connection refused, so every module-cache download and every Xcode CAS operation hangs until its own timeout. Measured 2026-08-10..08-14: 17 of 17 macOS sessions over 40 minutes started inside an episode, three hit the 6-hour ceiling, ~34h wall-clock burned. Meanwhile kura looks perfectly healthy: 0 restarts, no 5xx, almost no traffic.

Likely causes of a genuine single-node episode:
- Duplicated 'anchor "tuist.runners"' block in the host's /etc/pf.conf makes pfctl reject the WHOLE ruleset, dropping nat-anchor "com.apple/*" so the VM NAT anchor is never evaluated. Check: grep -c 'anchor "tuist.runners"' /etc/pf.conf (2 healthy, 4 broken), and pfctl -s nat (healthy shows nat-anchor "com.apple/*"). The vmnat anchor's CONTENTS can look perfect while nothing consults them.
- The host's PN VLAN lost its DHCP lease, so there is no PN route and traffic falls back to the default NIC.
- A tailnet route covering 172.16.0.0/22 pulling cache traffic off the VLAN.

Finding the culprit host: cilium_drop_count_total carries no source address. hubble_drop_total carries source/destination, but ONLY on clusters that have drop:sourceContext=pod|ip;destinationContext=pod applied from infra/k8s/mgmt/bootstrap/cilium-values.yaml — as of 2026-08-19 production does NOT, so that label is empty there. Fallback that works from metrics alone, since a mis-sourced host's PN VLAN goes nearly silent:

  sort_desc(max_over_time((sum by (instance) (rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{job="tuist-macos-node-exporter", device="vlan0"}[30m])))[7d:30m]))

Healthy runners-fleet minis peak in the hundreds of kB/s; the broken host in the August 2026 incident sat ~1600x below its peers. Use a 7-DAY peak, not a shorter window (a merely idle host looks broken over 6h) and not a floor or minimum. Scope to the runner fleet: macos-fleet and builders-fleet hosts sit at a couple hundred B/s legitimately, running no cache-using VMs.

Dashboard: /d/tuist-kura
annotations.summary: Kura cache on {{ $labels.node }} ({{ $labels.cluster }}) is dropping runner traffic at the NetworkPolicy: {{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.2f" }} denied packets/s

model.expr: sum by (cluster, node) (rate(cilium_drop_count_total{direction="INGRESS", reason="Policy denied"}[5m]) * on (cluster, pod) group_left(node) kube_pod_info{namespace="kube-system", pod=~"cilium-.*", node=~".*-kura-fleet-.*"})

annotations.description:
This host is reporting node_exporter metrics but has no vlan* network device, so installVMCachePNInterface has not run or the Private Network attachment is gone. Every PROVIDER-BACKED macOS host has exactly one.

Rack-owned hosts are excluded by the instance regex, and that exclusion is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. A StaticAppleSiliconMachine is a Mac mini in a rack we operate; it has no Scaleway Private Network and never will, so it correctly has no vlan device and fired this rule as critical the day the first one joined (2026-09-09). When BER1 gains its in-rack kura region the cache path will be in-rack L2, not a Scaleway PN, so the check for it is a NEW rule against whatever that path exposes, not a widening of this one. Do not remove the exclusion to 'cover the rack'; it would only restore the false positive.

Why this needs its own alert: it is the one cache-path failure the 'Kura Cache Rejecting Runner Traffic' alert cannot see. That alert detects VM traffic ARRIVING at the kura node mis-sourced and being policy-denied. With no VLAN there is no PN route at all, so cache traffic falls to the default route, is deliberately excluded from the general-internet masquerade (it would otherwise leave with the host's public source), and dies at the upstream gateway as an RFC1918 destination. It never reaches the kura node, the policy-drop counter stays at zero, and the build hangs exactly the same way, until its client timeout, which on the legacy CAS lane means hours. Without this rule the only witness is a stderr line in /var/log/tuist-pfctl-vmnat.log on the host itself, while the Node stays Ready and schedulable.

Nothing re-converges this on its own: the operator's drift loop keys on desired config, not live host state, so a host in this condition keeps taking jobs indefinitely.

What to do: SSH the host over the tailnet (Node InternalIP, user m1, key in Secret tuist-tuist-runners-fleet-ssh). `ifconfig -l | tr ' ' '\n' | grep vlan` to confirm, `tail /var/log/tuist-pfctl-vmnat.log` for the daemon's own complaint, and check the machine's Private Network attachment in Scaleway. Re-running the host bootstrap recreates the interface; `/usr/local/bin/tuist-pf-vmnat` then reloads the NAT within its 60s interval.

Known residual gap: this detects the DEVICE being absent, not a device that exists but has lost its DHCP address. node_exporter runs here without the netclass collector, so there is no node_network_up for vlan devices to key an address-level check on. A VLAN present but unaddressed has no PN route either and is still invisible to both alerts.

Dashboard: /d/tuist-runners
annotations.summary: macOS host {{ $labels.instance }} has no PN VLAN interface, so VM cache traffic cannot be NAT'd onto the Private Network

model.expr: count by (instance) (node_load1{job="tuist-macos-node-exporter", instance!~".*-rack-fleet-.*"}) unless count by (instance) (node_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="tuist-macos-node-exporter", device=~"vlan.*"})

annotations.description:
{{ $values.A.Value }} job(s) on {{ $labels.fleet }} have a ClickHouse runner_jobs row still reading queued/claimed/running while the authoritative Postgres runner_workflow_jobs row is terminal. The gauge already excludes anything younger than a 5-minute settle window, so genuinely in-flight jobs and normal outbox lag are not counted. Steady state is 0.

Why this matters: Postgres is the control plane and ClickHouse is a replica fed from the transition outbox. Divergence is supposed to be transient, because the flusher inserts into ClickHouse before deleting the outbox row inside one transaction, so a failure re-flushes byte-identical rows. A value that persists past the settle window means a replica row that will NOT converge on its own: a terminal job emits no further outbox events, so nothing lands to correct it.

The damage is not just a wrong status column. Runners.Analytics.jobs_duration filters on status = completed AND started_at/completed_at being non-null, so a job stuck non-terminal is silently dropped from customer-facing duration averages and percentiles, and from success and failure counts. The Jobs dashboard shows it as perpetually running.

This exists because the failure mode it watches for ran undetected for over a day on 2026-08-19: the log archiver copied a pre-terminal ClickHouse row forward under a newer updated_at, outranking the completion under the ReplacingMergeTree argMax. Runner queue age caught only the small queued slice (17 rows) and was blind to the running slice (794).

Likely causes:
- A new direct ClickHouse write to runner_jobs that does not source its lifecycle columns from Postgres. This is the one that has actually happened. Any code path calling IngestRepo.insert_all on Tuist.Runners.Job outside FlushJobTransitionEventsWorker is a suspect.
- The outbox flusher wedged for longer than the settle window, e.g. ClickHouse unreachable so the transaction keeps rolling back. Check the outbox depth in Postgres (runner_workflow_job_transition_events) and Oban for FlushJobTransitionEventsWorker failures. This case self-heals once the flusher recovers.
- A transition event whose payload lost a field in the JSONB round-trip, so the replayed row does not carry the status forward.

Not this: dispatch, capacity, or the autoscaler. Dispatch reads Postgres directly and is unaffected by replica state, so jobs keep running normally while this fires. It is a data-correctness alert, not an availability one.

Confirm and scope it with:

annotations.description:
OVHDedicatedMachine {{ $labels.machine }} in {{ $labels.cluster }} asked for spec.kataRuntime, but its Node carries no katacontainers.io/kata-runtime label. The kata-qemu RuntimeClass selects on exactly that label, so no runner Pod can schedule on this box. Meanwhile the Node is Ready, correctly pooled and tainted, and running all its DaemonSets, so nothing else looks wrong.

Why this needs its own alert: no other runner rule can see it. 'Runner Machine Stuck Failed' keys on the machine phase, which is Ready here, and a fleet-count check passes because the box exists and is healthy. On 2026-08-31 production and canary both reached this state and it read as a scheduling bug for about an hour.

Cause is almost always the once-at-bootstrap trap: the Linux self-join is rendered once, by whichever provider pod held the leader lease at that moment, and nothing re-runs it. During a rolling provider upgrade the outgoing pod keeps the lease until it terminates, so a Machine created in that window is bootstrapped by a build that does not understand the field and silently drops it. The fleets also use strategy: OnDelete, so flipping the field on later never rolls existing machines either.

The provider repairs this in place on the Ready path, so a brief 0 right after a box joins is normal and will not reach 20m. This rule firing means the repair itself is not converging.

What to do: read the KataRuntimeReady condition on the machine, which carries the reason.

  kubectl get ovhdedicatedmachine {{ $labels.machine }} -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="KataRuntimeReady")]}'

KataRuntimeMissing means the repair has not completed yet, or is deferred because the Node reports no InternalIP. KataRuntimeRepairFailed carries the actual failure: an unreachable box, or one whose containerd config predates 'version = 3', which the kata handler cannot be registered against.

Do NOT run 'kubectl delete machine' to force a re-bootstrap. That wipes the box, and on a cache node it destroys node-local state. Fix what the condition names and let the in-place repair land.

Only machines that asked for kata publish this series, so cache fleets never match. The series returns to 1 as soon as the repair succeeds.

Severity is warning rather than critical because this is lost capacity on one box, not broken builds, and a fleet-wide occurrence surfaces faster through 'Runner queue age'.

annotations.description:
Linux runner pool {{ $labels.fleet }} in {{ $labels.cluster }} has had dispatchable queued jobs (queue length minus jobs withheld by the account cap) for 10 minutes while the pool has zero Pods of any phase. Healthy state is a Pod being created within seconds of a queued job; a pool that has work and nothing at all is being refused creation.

Why this matters: the Linux provisioning admission budgets Pending Pods across every pool that shares a fleet (default 4). A sibling shape whose Pods cannot fit any node (the autoscaler targeted more replicas of an 18.5 GiB shape than the fleet seats) keeps those Pods Pending on Insufficient memory, holds the whole budget, and every other shape is refused creation for as long as the shortfall lasts. On 2026-09-02 linux-2vcpu-8gb sat at zero Pods for over an hour with 143 tuist-linux jobs queued, one of them the production cascade's own first job, so nothing could deploy; an hour later the mirror image happened (linux-2vcpu-8gb targeted at 87 held the budget and linux-4vcpu-16gb sat at zero with 17 queued). The queue-age alert fired but only after 30 minutes and without naming the mechanism; this fires at 10 and does.

Confirm: the runners-controller logs `Linux provisioning admission left replica gap` for the starved pool with reason=fleet_cap or pool_share and creating=0; `kubectl get runnerpools -n tuist-runners` shows the starved pool with replicas > 0 and no Pods, and a sibling with far more replicas than the fleet seats for its shape (tuist_runners_pool_phase_replicas by pool and phase).

Likely causes:
- A sibling shape's autoscaling.maxReplicas is above what the fleet can seat, so its Pods consume the shared admission budget continuously. Check tuist_runners_pool_pending_provisioning_pods by pool and tuist_runners_pool_admission_blocked_total by reason.
- The fleet lost nodes (tuist_runners_fleet_ready_nodes) and every shape is now oversubscribed.
- A node is Ready but cannot start any sandbox (FailedCreatePodSandBox with no space left on device under /data/containerd): see the 2026-09-02 ENOSPC incident notes.

What to do: cap the hogging pool at the fleet's seat count for its shape (kubectl patch runnerpool <pool> -n tuist-runners --type merge -p '{"spec":{"autoscaling":{"maxReplicas":N}}}'), which takes effect after its scale-down cooldown (300s); then make sure infra/helm/tuist/values-managed-production.yaml carries that bound so Helm owns it.

Not this: an account parked at its concurrency limit. Those jobs are subtracted via tuist_runners_queue_withheld.

Query notes: these metrics are served through Grafana Cloud adaptive aggregation, so the Pod leg aggregates by pool before renaming the label (a label_replace on the raw series returns nothing and the unless leg silently stops suppressing). The Pod leg uses tuist_runners_pool_phase_replicas, which counts actual Pods by phase; tuist_runners_pool_replicas_observed mirrors a status field that has read blank for pools that had Pods.

annotations.description:
No healthy node in the Linux runner fleet has had room for a {{ $labels.shape }} Pod for 10 minutes, while jobs the server is willing to dispatch have been queued for that shape. The fleet is not refusing to create Pods; it has nowhere to put them.

Why this needs its own rule: free memory summed across the fleet cannot answer 'can this fleet seat this shape'. On 2026-09-07 at 17:00 the four OVH RISE-L hosts in gra (117.135 GiB allocatable each, 31 vCPU) held roughly 38 GiB free between them, which by a fleet-wide byte budget affords one 16vcpu-32gb Pod and its contiguous 34.5 GiB (32 plus the kata RuntimeClass's 2.5 GiB podFixed). The largest single-node hole was 20 GiB and the real answer was zero. A job sat queued from 16:11 and was claimed at 17:10, the first moment two nodes could seat it. Sampling 12:00-20:00 that day, no node could seat that shape for 15.2% of the window and only one node could for a further 6.1%. This rule would have fired around 16:20, against the queue-age rule's 16:41.

The seat side is tuist_runners_fleet_shape_seats_free, published by the runners-controller every autoscaler reconcile. Per healthy node it takes allocatable minus what that node's Pods already reserve, divides by the shape's placement footprint, and sums the per-node quotients. It is never a fleet-wide total divided at the end. The footprint includes the RuntimeClass podFixed, and a running Pod is charged the same overhead from its own spec.overhead, so both sides of the division agree. Cordoned, NotReady and pressured nodes contribute zero.

First question: fragmentation or exhaustion? Read the whole shape ladder, not just the alerting rung:

  max by (cluster, shape) (tuist_runners_fleet_shape_seats_free{env="production", operating_system="linux"})

Smaller rungs still showing seats while the large ones read zero is fragmentation, the memory exists but not in one piece. Everything at zero is genuine exhaustion.

Then find what is holding the fleet (kubectl get pods -n tuist-runners -o wide --sort-by=.spec.nodeName). On 2026-09-07 it was a single account running uncapped at 384-464 GB peak daily against a ~467 GiB fleet; tightening its Linux limit to 64 vCPU / 128 GB at 17:19 took the fleet to a ~62% peak. Three other things routinely eat the same room:
- Terminating Pods. A kata sandbox whose shim never tore the microVM down keeps its node's memory reserved. The gauge counts them on purpose, because they really do hold the host. kubectl get pods -n tuist-runners --no-headers | grep Terminating
- A warm floor. minWarmPoolFloor on linux-2vcpu-8gb reserves floor * 10.5 GiB whether or not those Pods ever take a job. At 30 it held 315 GiB of a ~467 GiB fleet and left no 16 GiB hole; it is 4 now.
- Nodes out of the fleet. tuist_runners_fleet_ready_nodes below the MachineDeployment replica count, with tuist_runners_fleet_filtered_nodes naming the reason.

Not this:
- An account at its concurrency limit. The queue side subtracts tuist_runners_queue_withheld, so jobs the server is deliberately declining to dispatch do not count.
- The provisioning ceiling. tuist_runners_fleet_provisioning_ceiling is a concurrent-start budget, how many sandboxes may be booting at once. A fleet can be well inside it and still have nowhere to put the next Pod.
- Nodes leaving the fleet, which shows on tuist_runners_fleet_ready_nodes first and lowers seats as a consequence.
- A phantom queue on its own. tuist_runners_queue_length currently counts jobs that are in fact running (a displaced job never leaves queued), but that cannot fire this rule by itself: the seat side has to independently read zero, and it is computed from live node allocatable and live Pod requests without touching the queue. What the inflation CAN do is make this fire on a fleet that is fully committed and healthy. Until that bug is fixed, cross-check tuist_runners_autoscaler_queued_jobs for the shape before treating a firing as a capacity shortfall.

Severity is warning rather than critical: a fleet with no room for its largest shape at peak is saturation, not a fault, and it clears when a job finishes. 'Runner pool starved' (10m, zero Pods of any phase) and 'Runner queue age' (30m of queue age) remain the critical rules for the case where it does not clear. No affected_service for the same reason, a saturated fleet is not a status-page outage.

Query note: these series pass through Grafana Cloud adaptive aggregation, which has taken instance and pod off the queue gauges. A label_replace on the raw selector therefore ERRORS rather than returning nothing, which is why the queue leg aggregates by (cluster, env, fleet) INSIDE the label_replace. If this rule ever shows Error, check whether shape or fleet_selector has been aggregated off tuist_runners_fleet_shape_seats_free; the fix is the keep_labels escape hatch, not deleting the recommendation.

annotations.summary: ClickHouse query {{ $labels.query_hash }} was slow or cancelled {{ $values.A }} times in 15 minutes: {{ $labels.query_preview }}

model.rawSql:
SELECT
  toString(normalized_query_hash) AS query_hash,
  substring(replaceRegexpAll(normalizeQuery(any(query)), '\\s+', ' '), 1, 120) AS query_preview,
  countIf(type = 'ExceptionWhileProcessing' AND exception_code IN (394, 210, 159))
    + countIf(type = 'QueryFinish' AND query_duration_ms >= 10000) AS slow_or_cancelled
FROM clusterAllReplicas('default', system.query_log)
WHERE event_time >= now() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
  AND type IN ('QueryFinish', 'ExceptionWhileProcessing')
  AND is_initial_query
  AND http_user_agent LIKE 'ch/%'
GROUP BY query_hash
HAVING slow_or_cancelled > 0
ORDER BY slow_or_cancelled DESC
LIMIT 20

annotations.description:
Build ingestion jobs have exhausted all 5 attempts and been discarded. Discarded jobs are never retried, and Oban prunes them, so every one of these is permanently lost customer build data once pruning catches up.

WHY THIS RULE WAS REWRITTEN ON 2026-09-09. It previously read tuist_oban_jobs_recent_terminal_count, a metric that is emitted nowhere in the codebase and has never existed in Prometheus. The rule sat in Normal (NoData) from 2026-06-19 until 2026-09-09, and because No Data was mapped to OK that silence was indistinguishable from health. It was therefore dead through the 2026-09-09 build ingestion outage, in which 1,629 jobs were discarded over 3.4 hours and roughly 30 were pruned before recovery. Before changing this expression, run it and confirm it returns a series.

DO NOT REWRITE THIS ONTO rate() OR increase(). The Oban job counters (tuist_oban_job_exception_attempts_count and friends) are subject to Grafana Cloud adaptive metrics, which aggregates away instance and pod. Measured on 2026-09-09 at 5m, 15m, 1h and 6h windows, and again evaluated mid-outage, rate() and increase() over those aggregated counters return an EMPTY result rather than an error. A rule built on them is silently dead in exactly the way this one was. The polled gauge below is not a counter and does not have that problem.

What the value means: it is the number of rows currently in oban_jobs with state=discarded for this queue, not a rate. It stays elevated until Oban prunes them, which is intended, because the actionable question is whether discarded build data is sitting there right now.

Threshold rationale: over the 14 days to 2026-09-09 this gauge had p50 0, p95 3 and p99 7 on production, against a peak of 1,650 during the outage. 25 sits about 3.5x above p99 and was crossed by roughly 11:10 UTC, about 15 minutes after the first error.

No Data is Alerting here on purpose, which is the opposite of most rules in this folder. The gauge is polled from the shared oban_jobs table by every node running Tuist.Oban.PromExPlugin, so it is present whenever any server pod is up and it emits an explicit zero for a queue that drains. Its absence therefore means the telemetry broke, which is the failure this rule spent three months in. The 10 minute pending period is what keeps a deploy roll from paging.

Most likely cause, seen three times: Tuist.Release.do_grant_processor_role revokes all table privileges from the tuist_processor role on every migrate and re-grants only the hardcoded @processor_read_tables and @processor_write_tables lists in server/lib/tuist/release.ex. A new table read on the ingestion path that is missing from those lists fails every job with Postgrex 42501 insufficient_privilege. Previous recurrences were webhook_endpoints, then automation_alerts, then feature_flags.

Confirm:
  SELECT state, count(*) FROM oban_jobs WHERE queue = 'process_build' GROUP BY 1;
And read the actual error off a discarded row's errors array.

annotations.description:
An Oban consumer of {{ $labels.queue }} started a job in the last 15 minutes and did not finish one in the last 15 minutes. It is claiming work and destroying it.

Why this exists separately from 'Remote processing queue has no consumer': that rule keys on the queue, which is correct when EVERY consumer is gone and blind when one of several is broken. Healthy peers keep the queue drained, so depth, queue age and every readiness signal read perfectly normal while a fraction of jobs is quietly lost.

On 2026-08-25 one of the two production xcresult processors blocked on every parse for the full 600s NIF deadline. It completed zero jobs for fourteen hours while its sibling completed 84 to 218 an hour. Nothing fired. The Pod was 1/1 Running with zero restarts, up was 1, the PDB was satisfied, and queue age sat at 0 throughout. It was found by hand from oban_jobs.attempted_by.

Read the expression as: started a job recently, did not finish one recently. Both halves are load-bearing. Without the attempt clause an idle node on a quiet queue looks identical to a wedged one, because time-since-last-completion climbs in both cases. 'unless' rather than 'and' is what covers a node that wedges BEFORE its first completion: that node has no completion series at all, and 'and' against a missing series matches nothing.

Healthy state is an empty result, so this runs with No Data: Normal. A consumer that stops serving metrics entirely produces no series here rather than firing; that case is covered by the 'xcresult processor guest metrics unavailable' rules, which key on up.

WHY THE PENDING PERIOD IS 20 MINUTES, NOT 5. A Pod that is being drained keeps a recent last_attempt while it stops completing, and its series does not disappear when the Pod does: the host-side :9091 forwarder caches the guest's metrics, so a dead Pod's last sample outlives it. On 2026-08-31 this paged for xcresult-processor-b24xg roughly five minutes AFTER a release deploy had already deleted it. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30, so the Pod itself was long gone; the whole firing window was stale data. Measured, that stale window sustains the condition for about 10 minutes. 20 minutes is twice that, and a genuinely wedged consumer holds the condition for hours, so nothing real is lost.

A pod-existence join (kube_pod_status_phase) was considered and rejected: it only trims the tail (a terminating Pod is still phase=Running), and making a critical rule depend on kube-state-metrics means it goes silently dead if KSM breaks, which is the exact 14-hours-undetected failure this rule exists to prevent.

BEFORE TREATING THIS AS A WEDGE, CHECK THE POD STILL EXISTS:
  kubectl --context tuist-k8s-production get pods -n tuist | grep xcresult
If the node named here is not in that list, this is a stale page from a rolled Pod.

15 minutes in the expression is safe against a legitimately slow job: the NIF's own parse deadline is 600s plus a 30s cancellation grace, so a single slow parse cannot reach it.

Confirm and identify:
  SELECT state, attempted_by[1] AS node, count(*)
  FROM oban_jobs WHERE queue = '{{ $labels.queue }}' GROUP BY 1, 2;
Do NOT read a missing 'completed' row as proof of a gap: completed jobs are pruned aggressively and the table holds only a handful even on a healthy fleet. Use tuist_oban_node_last_completion_timestamp_seconds, or the hourly parse_timeout rate from the errors array.

Distinguishing a wedge from genuine slowness: a wedged parse burns no CPU. Check host load on the mini before assuming saturation.

Remediation: delete the Pod so tart-kubelet boots a fresh Tart VM, ONE AT A TIME (the PDB is minAvailable: 1), and verify the replacement actually COMPLETES jobs before touching the next — tart-kubelet has no container probe, so 1/1 Running proves nothing. Note this destroys the evidence, so capture what you can first.

See also 'Remote processing consumer is losing its slots', which catches the same decay hours earlier by comparing in-flight jobs against the configured queue limit.

annotations.description:
An Oban consumer is holding fewer in-flight jobs than its configured queue limit, while more than 100 jobs sit available for it to take. It is losing capacity.

Why this exists alongside 'Remote processing queue consumer takes work but completes none': that rule is correct but fires only once the consumer has stopped completing work ENTIRELY. On 2026-08-31 that was about a day after the decay started and roughly 3000 unprocessed test runs into it.

That day both production xcresult processors were holding 3 in-flight jobs against a configured limit of 6, with thousands of jobs available to fill the gap. Deleting the Pods restored both to 6 immediately. The capacity leaks: a parse that hits the NIF's outer deadline (600s + 30s grace) never gives its slot back, so a processor's usable concurrency only ever decreases across the Pod's lifetime. Sentry TUIST-4JE shows the same decay by generation: Pods that lived 0.5 to 16 hours logged 1 to 13 timeouts each, while the two that reached 69 hours logged 670 and 429.

A consumer at half capacity still completes jobs on the slots it still has, so the liveness pair, queue depth, queue age and up all read healthy while it decays. These two gauges are the only ones that move while there is still time to act.

The backlog clause is what makes this safe. A node under its limit is completely normal when there is nothing to run; it is only a defect when work is waiting and the node still will not take it.

Warning rather than critical, at a 15 minute pending period, because the whole point is that it fires with hours of headroom. The critical rule remains the backstop for the case where this is missed and throughput reaches zero.

Confirm and identify:
  SELECT attempted_by[1] AS node, count(*)
  FROM oban_jobs WHERE queue = '{{ $labels.queue }}' AND state = 'executing'
  GROUP BY 1;
Compare each node against xcresultProcessor.queueConcurrency in infra/helm/tuist/values-managed-production.yaml (6 in production). Below it = slots have leaked. Equal = healthy.

Remediation: delete the Pod so tart-kubelet boots a fresh Tart VM. Do them ONE AT A TIME, the PDB is minAvailable: 1. Verify the replacement actually COMPLETES jobs before touching the next: tart-kubelet has no container probe, so 1/1 Running proves nothing here.

Note this is mitigation, not a fix. Expect recurrence 24-48h after every roll until the NIF stops leaking slots on its outer deadline path.

annotations.description:
Builds uploaded by the CLI are queued for ingestion and are not being consumed. This is the leading indicator for the failure mode the discarded-jobs rule only catches once retries are exhausted: it turns positive as soon as work stops draining, roughly an hour before jobs start being destroyed.

WHY THIS RULE EXISTS. On 2026-09-09 build ingestion failed for 3.4 hours. Every job raised Postgrex 42501 insufficient_privilege inside Tuist.Builds.create_build/1, 1,629 jobs exhausted 5 attempts and were discarded, and roughly 30 were pruned before recovery and are permanently lost. The CLI saw none of it: uploads returned 2xx throughout, so HTTP error rate, latency and availability all stayed green while 100 percent of ingestion was failing. No request-level rule can see this class of outage, because the data is destroyed asynchronously after the response is sent.

THIS RULE IS DELIBERATELY SCOPED TO ONE QUEUE. Do not generalise it across queues with a shared threshold. Measured over the 14 days to 2026-09-09 on production, the default queue sits at an oldest-available age of about 61 days as a matter of course, and process_xcresult has a p95 of roughly 5 hours because it legitimately runs long backlogs. A fleet-wide threshold is either permanently firing or useless. A sibling rule for another queue needs its own baseline.

Threshold rationale: for process_build this gauge had p50 0, p95 0 and p99 60 seconds over that window. 300 seconds is 5x p99. During the outage it crossed 300 at roughly 12:20 UTC and climbed to 690 seconds by the time the incident was mitigated by hand.

AVAILABLE age, not raw queue depth. This measures how long the oldest job that is ready to run has been waiting, so a backlog that is being worked through steadily does not fire, and a queue with a live consumer that has stopped completing does.

No Data is OK here because the paired rule 'ProcessBuildWorker - jobs being discarded' runs with No Data set to Alerting over the same plugin, so a telemetry failure is already loud once and does not need to page twice.

Most likely cause, seen three times: Tuist.Release.do_grant_processor_role revokes all table privileges from the tuist_processor role on every migrate and re-grants only the hardcoded lists in server/lib/tuist/release.ex, so a new table read on the ingestion path that is missing from those lists fails every job. Previous recurrences were webhook_endpoints, then automation_alerts, then feature_flags.

Confirm:
  SELECT state, count(*) FROM oban_jobs WHERE queue = 'process_build' GROUP BY 1;
Then read the error off a retryable or discarded row's errors array.

See also 'Remote processing queue consumer takes work but completes none', which keys on individual consumers and fired correctly throughout the 2026-09-09 outage.

annotations.description: One of the egress-tree agent's tripwires fired on a governed box. unshaped_packets: traffic reached the tree unclassified (a hand-cleared root qdisc runs unshaped until the backstop rebuild). return_drops: shaped packets dropped for missing metadata, pods blackholed. return_attach_failures: the return program failed to attach, shaped pods blackholed until the detach threshold. reconcile_errors: the loop is failing. sibling_overflow: an account outgrew the 16-entry sibling map, extra replicas run shaped with no log. reattach_churn: a tcx link the agent had already installed was stripped or displaced from the head of a pod device's chain. Cilium replaces its own link in place and leaves ours alone, so this means external interference; the matching 'reattached pod program' warning in the agent log names the pod and device. CAVEAT on agent versions older than the metric split (those not exporting kura_egress_tree_link_attach_total): there this counter ALSO counted the first attach on every new pod device, so any kura rollout replaces every pod, each replacement gets a new lxc device, and this signal trips with nothing wrong. annotations.description:
New Kura instances still reach their accounts, but slower than they should. This is not a stall: the two rules next to it (provisioned but not serving, stalled in provisioning) cover an instance that never serves, on a 15-minute threshold. This one is the speed of the ones that do, so it catches drift in DNS publication, local-path volume provisioning, the regional gateway's sync rate, or image pulls on a box that has never run the tag.

WHAT THE VALUE IS. tuist_kura_lifecycle_new_instance_time_to_ready_p90_seconds is a PromEx polling gauge, recomputed every five minutes from kura_deployments over the last 24 hours: per account-region instance that started serving, the wall-clock from the deployment that brought it up to its endpoint answering. First provisions and cold returns only, which is the first deployment a server has had since its account-region last returned from archive. Fleet rollouts mint about ten times as many deployments and pass through the same activation path, so they are excluded or they would measure the rollout gate instead.

READ IT WITH max, NOT sum. Every tuist-tuist-server replica reports the same fleet-wide value and Adaptive Metrics has aggregated instance and pod away, so sum multiplies it by the replica count.

WHY THE SAMPLE GATE. The rule only evaluates while the window holds at least 10 new instances; production provisions on the order of 30 a day. The gauge is not emitted at all when the window is empty, which is why No Data is OK: a fleet that provisioned nothing has no speed to report.

WHERE TO LOOK FIRST. Take one recent instance and read its timeline: the server logs 'waiting on DNS for server' and 'waiting on public endpoint for server' from AwaitActivationWorker while it polls, and the kura namespace's pod and volume events give provisioning and readiness times. external-dns logs in the platform namespace show when the record reached Cloudflare; it syncs about 5 seconds after a change, and Cloudflare itself has taken 5 to 10 seconds to answer a new record.

WHY 120 SECONDS. Production's p90 for a first provision was 181s the week before the on-demand provisioning work, and a staging drill of the same path afterwards returned an archived instance in 13.7s. Tighten toward 60s once a couple of weeks of production data exist.

A refused account stays on whatever lane it was on and raises nothing else. The value is negative when reservations already sit above the line. Check "Kura - admission refusing instances" for what is being turned down, then free reservations (archive instances that store nothing) or add a node to the region's pool. The second operand of the query is the same arithmetic without the kura_servers rows, used until tuist_kura_capacity_admission_headroom_gibibytes is exported. annotations.description:
This counts IN-PLACE container restarts, so a rollout cannot trigger it: a replacement pod starts its counter at zero. The container was killed by the kubelet after 'Container kura failed liveness probe'. Expect Reason=Error and exit code 137, never OOMKilled - a rule keyed on OOMKilled sees none of this.

Why this went unalerted for weeks: the generic 'Pod restarts (possible overload)' rule is scoped namespace="tuist" and never covered namespace="kura" at all, and both generic thresholds (>2 in 15m, >5 in 1h) sit far above this fault's rate anyway.

ROOT CAUSE HAS TWO CONTRIBUTORS AND ONLY ONE IS FIXED. Read this before concluding the alert is stale.

(1) CAS segment eviction monopolised a worker. Store::evict_segment scanned a full 512 MiB segment's artifact index in a single poll, plus a prefix scan and two reads per cascaded action-cache entry, committing it all as one batch. Fixed in PR #12553 (yields every 256 rows, budget shared with the cascade scan).

(2) The write-buffer stall, NOT fixed, and this is what scales (1) to the whole process. resolve_worker_threads() gives production 16 tokio workers, and one parked worker out of 16 cannot fail three /up probes over ~60s. What can: the metadata store is built with allow_stall=true on a 32 MiB WriteBufferManager shared with the block cache, so on saturation RocksDB blocks EVERY thread inside db.write in FFI, and those calls run directly on tokio workers. Measured: the write-buffer ratio peaked at 1.126 on kura-tuist-scw-fr-par-0 and kura-tuist-eu-central-1-0 against a 0.844 healthy peak elsewhere, and those are the same two pods that recorded up=0 mid-stall. On eu-central-1-0 the failed scrape at 16:25:00 precedes its Killing event at 16:25:26, so /metrics was down while the process still ran: the whole listener, not one route. Tracked in issue #12556.

SO: if this keeps firing after #12553 lands, that is EXPECTED unless #12556 also landed. Check 'Kura - metadata store write buffer saturated' alongside - it is the instrument that decides. The eviction feeds the stall it then waits inside (its 20k-30k-delete batch is one large charge against that same 32 MiB pool), and the batch cannot be chunked because the cascade must stay atomic, so yielding does not reduce the charge.

Log signature: a 'cascaded action-cache entries stranded by segment eviction' line, then 49-63 seconds of silence, then 'received SIGUSR1' as the preStop hook fires. Cascade SIZE does not predict it: 47 and 305 entries stalled the pod exactly as 4,555 and 7,360 did.

Why a restart is not a cheap recovery: the node leaves the mesh, and on return every peer runs catch-up backfill against it (one pass applied 27,716 artifacts and 545 MB). That write burst rotates segments, which evicts, which stalls again, so restarts cluster and the single-replica runner-facing cache is worst hit.

Threshold rationale: backtested over 7 days across all 30 production Kura pods at 10-minute sampling, >=2 restarts in 6h held true at 304/45/35 sample points for the three affected pods and was NEVER true for the other 27. The [1h] variant is equally specific but held at only 1 and 3 points for two of the three, because restarts arrive in clusters hours apart.
