annotations.description:
This is the MECHANISM behind 'Kura - cache pod restart loop', and the only one of the Kura stall rules visible BEFORE the pod stops answering.

Kura builds its metadata store with a RocksDB WriteBufferManager whose stall flag is enabled (kura/src/store.rs, new_write_buffer_manager_with_cache(pool, true, cache)). Once memtable memory reaches the pool size, RocksDB blocks every thread inside its write call until a flush drains it. Those write calls run directly on tokio worker threads rather than on the blocking pool, so a saturated write buffer parks the runtime itself: the probe handlers stop being scheduled even though /up reads nothing but process-local config and takes no lock.

The squeeze is configuration. KURA_METADATA_STORE_WRITE_BUFFER_POOL_BYTES is hardcoded to 32 MiB in BOTH kura/ops/helm/kura/values-managed.yaml and infra/kura-controller/controllers/kurainstance_controller.go, for every managed instance regardless of size. The process would otherwise derive memory_limit/32 clamped to [16,128] MiB, which is 128 MiB at the 4Gi limit these pods run, so the override is 4x tighter. The same allocation is shared with the block cache (READ_CACHE_BYTES is also 32 MiB and the manager is constructed WITH that cache), so memtable growth evicts the read cache that the eviction scan depends on.

The largest batch the store writes is CAS segment eviction, which deletes every artifact in a 512 MiB segment plus every action-cache entry cascading off those blobs in a single batch, and scans that whole segment index synchronously to build it.

THRESHOLD RATIONALE - busy is not the same as stalled. Over the 24 hours to 2026-08-21 the idle fleet baseline was 0.063, five healthy pods across three regions peaked at 0.844 under ordinary load, and exactly one pod exceeded the pool size at 1.125. A threshold at 0.9, and certainly one at 0.8, would page on the normal peak. 0.95 was chosen to sit between the measured normal peak and the one measured excursion, NOT from any property of RocksDB - re-measure the distribution before tightening it.

This gauge only exists while the pod is scrapeable, which is precisely the window this rule is for. Once the stall is underway the series stops arriving and the restart rule takes over.

annotations.description:
The paired telemetry rule for every Kura rule that reads a metric off the kura scrape job: kura_http_*, kura_rocksdb_* and kura_response_stream_admissions_*. Those are threshold rules with No Data: OK, so they cannot distinguish a healthy fleet from a scrape configuration that stopped discovering the kura namespace altogether. Without this rule, deleting the kura scrape job would silence them permanently and look identical to health.

Since 'Kura - cache pod failing scrapes' was retired on 2026-08-26, no rule reads up{job="kura"} directly any more. That does not weaken this rule or make it redundant: its subject was never up itself but the scrape job behind it, and the same job feeds every kura_* series the remaining rules depend on.

WHY EACH CLUSTER IS NAMED RATHER THAN A BARE up{job="kura"}: absent_over_time is absent-or-nothing across everything its selector matches, so the bare form stays empty while ANY cluster still has one Kura target. It could not see a single cluster's targets disappear, which is the case worth alerting on, and if it ever did fire the result would carry no cluster label for the summary to interpolate. Only equality matchers survive into the output of absent_over_time, so naming each cluster is also what puts cluster on the alert.

Kura runs in tuist-production, tuist-staging and tuist-canary, and deliberately not in tuist-management. ADD A DISJUNCT WHEN A NEW CLUSTER STARTS HOSTING KURA - a cluster absent from this list is silently uncovered.

Note the polarity, which is the opposite of a normal threshold rule: absent_over_time returns 1 when the series has been absent for the whole window and returns NOTHING when it is present. So the healthy state here is an empty result, which is why No Data must be OK and NOT Alerting - setting No Data to Alerting would make this fire continuously while the fleet is healthy. Error is set to Alerting, because an evaluation error genuinely means this safety net is not working. The same inversion applies to every other absent_over_time rule in alerts.md; the document's step-8 guidance used to say the opposite.

Production normally has around 30 targets on this job, staging around 22 and canary 1, so this only fires when a whole cluster's worth vanishes. That is a monitoring-pipeline failure, not a cache failure: check the Alloy metrics collector and the kura namespace's prometheus.io/scrape pod annotations before assuming an outage.

annotations.description: The instance's ring is full and it is evicting artifacts younger than a day (median age of the youngest artifact in each segment the ring rotated out over the last day). Overnight and weekend builds will miss. Rings run full by design; what this measures is whether the claim is enough for the account's write rate. The lever is the account's storage claim, which Tuist.Kura.ClaimSizing sizes and applies on its own, and it is usually still confirming the reading when this fires: its one-day rungs need two to five qualifying days before they grow the claim. Watch it; it escalates to "Kura instance retention horizon under a day for three days" if sizing does not land. Only rings that have been full for the whole day count: a ring rebuilt more recently cannot report an eviction older than itself, so it would fire on its own age.

annotations.description:
A per-account Kura StatefulSet is serving on fewer ready replicas than it declares, whatever took the replica away: unschedulable, crash-looping, stuck terminating, or a rollout that never finished.

Why this matters: every managed instance runs replicas: 2 so a deploy always has somewhere to hand traffic to, and the standby is also what a rebuilt replica refills its ring from over the peer mesh. An instance down to one replica still answers, which is why nothing that watches request rates or error rates sees anything. It is not an outage; it is the absence of the thing that keeps the next deploy from being one. On 2026-09-07 a kura-<account>-us-east-1-1 replica was found to have sat Pending for roughly two days while -0 served, with its PVC bound to a scw-local-nvme volume pinned to a box that had since filled.

Likely causes:
- A node-local PV pinning the replica to a box that has since filled. The volume carries a kubernetes.io/hostname affinity fixed on the day it first bound, so the replica cannot go anywhere else and adding a box to the region does not help it. Cross-check 'Kura box cannot take back its largest replica', which reads that condition before a replica departs.
- A crash loop. Cross-check 'Kura cache pod restart loop'.
- A rollout that has not finished, which is normal inside the 30-minute pending period and not after it.

What to do: kubectl -n kura get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=<statefulset> and kubectl -n kura describe pod on the missing ordinal. If it is Pending, read the FailedScheduling event for the per-reason node counts.

Repairing a pinned wedge: delete the replica's data PVC. The StatefulSet recreates it, WaitForFirstConsumer binds a fresh volume wherever the pod is placed rather than where the old one was, and the pod refills its ring from its sibling. About two minutes, with no customer-visible interruption, because the replica being replaced is Pending and serving nothing. Confirm the sibling is Ready first: the volume is one of the account's two copies and the replacement refills from the other one.

Expression note: written as a subtraction rather than ready < replicas so a healthy instance evaluates to an explicit 0. A comparison operator filters, which would leave a healthy fleet indistinguishable from a rule that has gone blind. Single-replica instances (the private runner-cache regions) are 1 - 1 = 0 and never match.
annotations.summary: Kura instance {{ $labels.statefulset }} has been short of ready replicas for 30 minutes in {{ $labels.cluster }} ({{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.0f" }} missing)

model.expr: kube_statefulset_replicas{namespace="kura"} - kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{namespace="kura"}

rules.title: Kura instance below its replica count

annotations.description:
A Kura box has committed so much of its tuist.dev/memory-ceiling-mib budget that if its largest replica left, it could not be placed back on this box. That matters because a Kura data volume is node-local and pins its replica here: the replica has nowhere else to go, so it sits Pending until somebody deletes the claim. This is the leading indicator for that wedge, and it is readable before any replica actually leaves.

The invariant: committed <= allocatable - largest single replica request. The value on this alert is how far past that line the box is, in MiB.

Why a seat is not simply held: Kubernetes accounts extended resources against scheduled pods, not against volumes. The moment a replica is deleted for any reason (a rollout, an eviction, a drain, a storage rebuild), its request stops being counted and another instance can take the headroom. Kura pods run at priority 0 with no PriorityClass, so the returning replica cannot preempt whatever took its seat; and on these boxes every competitor for the budget is another Kura pod, so a uniform PriorityClass would have nothing to preempt anyway.

What to do: this is a placement and capacity signal, not a pod fault. Add a box to the region, or move an instance out of it. Do NOT clear it by shrinking an account's memory profile, which is its floor, not its slack. Cross-check 'Kura region cannot place another instance', which describes the region rather than the individual box, and can be quiet while one box in the region is over this line.

If a replica has already wedged on this box, 'Kura instance below its replica count' fires too and carries the repair.

Known state on creation (2026-09-07): one production box sits about 950 MiB over the line, which is the box that produced the two-day single-replica wedge this rule exists to precede. It is expected to fire for that box until the region gains capacity.

Enforcement, as opposed to this warning, belongs in Tuist.Kura.Capacity and the admission path, alongside the egress_headroom accounting that already implements this shape for tuist.dev/egress-mbps.
annotations.summary: Kura box {{ $labels.node }} in {{ $labels.cluster }} is committed {{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.0f" }} MiB past the point where its largest replica could come back

model.expr: (sum by (cluster, node) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{namespace="kura", resource="tuist_dev_memory_ceiling_mib"}) + max by (cluster, node) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{namespace="kura", resource="tuist_dev_memory_ceiling_mib"})) - max by (cluster, node) (kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="tuist_dev_memory_ceiling_mib"})

rules.title: Kura box cannot take back its largest replica

annotations.description:
Cache resolution offers an account only its active instances, so an instance that never reaches active is one the account is allocated, is paying for, and is not routed to. It keeps building against the legacy cache-*.tuist.dev lane. Nothing errors and no build fails, which is exactly why no request-rate, error-rate or pod-health rule sees this: the KuraInstance is Ready, its pods answer, and the fault is in front of the workload.

READ THE VALUE WITH max, NOT sum. This is a PromEx polling gauge and every tuist-tuist-server replica reports the same fleet-wide count, so Adaptive Metrics has aggregated instance and pod away. sum returns the true count multiplied by the replica count (on 2026-09-08 it read 10 for us-east against a true 2); max returns the truth, because every replica reports the same number. region and cluster both survive the aggregation, so the per-region breakdown in this rule is real.

Why 30 minutes. Provisioning, replicating and failed all count here, and a healthy cold provision passes through in about 105 seconds (121s worst case over the 2026-09-08 cohort). The pending period is the whole of what separates ordinary fleet growth from an instance that is genuinely stuck, so do not shorten it below a few minutes.

FIRST THING TO CHECK is the account's TLS certificate, which is the cause of every occurrence so far:

  kubectl -n kura get certificate,order | grep -v True

Activation gates on the public endpoint answering /up over HTTPS. A certificate that was never issued leaves the ingress serving its default self-signed cert, the control plane's probe fails TLS verification on every reconciler tick, and the instance never activates while its KuraInstance reports 2/2 replicas Ready on the right image. On 2026-09-08 three accounts stalled this way at once because Let's Encrypt refused new certificates for tuist.dev under its 50-certificates-per-registered-domain weekly limit, which the Kura fleet's growth from roughly 23 to 64 tenants had exhausted. That limit is domain-wide, so it strands every newly provisioned tenant at once and clears only when the 168h window rolls.

Other causes: DNS that never propagated (external-dns), or a node-port chain the controller never completed. The reconciler names which one at info level in the server log, as 'waiting on DNS for server', 'waiting on public endpoint for server' or 'waiting on node-port endpoint for server'; search Loki for those. Past 15 minutes it also marks the server failed and captures 'Kura provisioning stalled' to Sentry with the reason and the region.

Read the instance status on /ops/kura. Do NOT restart the pod or destroy the instance: the workload is healthy in every case seen so far, and a teardown discards the account's cache content in that region for nothing.

annotations.description:
The regional Kura ingress controller has been answering clients of one Kura instance with a non-standard status (009 or 000, which clients see as HTTP/2 000, HTTP/0.9 or a protocol error) or with 502, sustained for 15 minutes. The upstream label is the instance's HTTP backend. Kura itself looks healthy while this happens: the access log line carries upstream status 200 next to client status 009, so no kura_* metric moves and neither Kura latency nor Kura 5xx rules fire.

Known cause: nginx reuses its upstream keepalive connections to pod port 4000 across the gRPC and HTTP Ingresses of the same instance. An HTTP request handed an h2c connection logs 'upstream sent no valid HTTP/1.0 header'; a gRPC call handed an HTTP/1.1 connection logs 'no connection data found for keepalive http2 connection' and answers 502. It only bites an instance serving both lanes at once (Xcode CAS or Bazel over gRPC plus module cache over HTTP). PR #13227 routes gateway gRPC to a dedicated Kura port; until it deploys, expect this to fire for accounts that mix both lanes.

Why it matters beyond the failed requests: the CLI's endpoint latency probe treats one failed GET /up as unreachable and moves the CAS proxy to another region for at least 10 minutes. Cross-check 'Xcode cache - CI remote reads slow for an account' for the same account.

Inspect in Loki (grafanacloud-logs): {service_name="<service_name>"} |= "[<upstream>]" |~ "\" (0[0-9]{2}|502) " for the requests, and {service_name="<service_name>"} |~ "no valid HTTP/1.0 header|no connection data found for keepalive" for the controller's error lines.

Scope: 503 and 504 are excluded. They come from draining pods, capacity shedding and upstream timeouts, arrive in bursts of thousands during deploys, and the Kura 5xx rule covers the ones Kura produces. The 15-minute pending period excludes isolated bursts: one burst stays inside the 15-minute window for three 5-minute evaluations and never reaches the fourth. Backtested 2026-09-01 to 09-15: fires for the incident instances throughout 2026-09-14/15 and a few times a week for two other instances with mixed lanes; single bursts, including one of 4,287 502s, did not fire.

Source: the controllers' access logs, which keep every line except sampled 2xx and 404. The kura-ingress-nginx Prometheus scrape (PR #13239) adds nginx_ingress_controller_requests for these controllers; this rule can move to it once that deploys.

annotations.description:
Leading indicator for "Kura shedding cache writes by kind" (the outbox kind). Once the outbox reaches its cap both write gates refuse public writes: HTTP answers 429 and the remote-execution surface answers gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED; the cache client only retries GETs, so a refused HTTP upload is lost rather than delayed. Do NOT assume an unreachable peer: check max by (pod) (kura_outbox_messages) and sum by (pod)

Drain is serial and node-wide, one delivery per peer round-trip, so a backlog is ingest outrunning it. If the write-shed rule is also firing the window has closed. The same backlog gates Kura runtime rollouts, so this pod is likely holding a rollout in wave 0.

annotations.description:
The in-cluster ClickHouse (or its Keeper) has had no ready replica for 10 minutes in {{ $labels.cluster }}.

Why this matters: during the migration off ClickHouse Cloud this server receives every mirrored write, and once reads are flipped onto it (FunWithFlags `clickhouse_bare_metal_reads`) it serves the dashboards. Keeper matters as much as the server: every table is a Replicated engine, so losing the quorum makes them read-only and writes fail rather than queue.

While it is down, mirrored writes are dropped by design and the destination falls behind. That gap is repaired by re-running the backfill with a later cutoff, which copies only the rows the destination lacks.

Likely causes:
- The bare-metal node is gone or NotReady (pool `clickhouse`, taint tuist.dev/stateful)
- The local PersistentVolume is not bound, so the pod cannot schedule
- A deploy from a branch that does not contain the managed ClickHouse: the chart then renders no StatefulSet and Helm deletes it. The data survives (the PV is Retain plus helm.sh/resource-policy: keep) and a deploy from a branch that does contain it brings the workload back.

Note NoData is deliberately not alerting: the workload does not exist in an environment that has not enabled it yet. Once it is permanently deployed everywhere, flip NoData to Alerting so that the workload disappearing is itself the alert.
annotations.summary: {{ $labels.statefulset }} has no ready replica in {{ $labels.cluster }}

model.expr: min by (cluster, statefulset) (kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{statefulset=~"tuist-tuist-clickhouse(-keeper)?"})

annotations.description:
A Replicated table on the in-cluster ClickHouse has been read-only for 5 minutes.

Why this matters: every table on this server is a Replicated engine, which keeps its metadata in ClickHouse Keeper. When a replica cannot reach the quorum it drops to read-only, and writes fail outright rather than queueing. The server keeps answering /ping and keeps serving reads, so nothing else notices: this metric is the signal.

During the migration that means mirrored writes are being dropped and the destination is falling behind. The gap is repaired by re-running the backfill with a later cutoff, which copies only the rows the destination lacks. After the cutover it means ingestion is failing outright.

Likely causes:
- Keeper has lost quorum, or its pod is down or unschedulable
- Network between the ClickHouse pod and the Keeper service
- Keeper's own volume is full

Where to look: the Keeper StatefulSet in the same namespace, then this pod's log for `Cannot get replica` or ZooKeeper session errors.
annotations.summary: {{ $value }} ClickHouse table(s) read-only on {{ $labels.pod }} ({{ $labels.cluster }})

model.expr: max by (cluster, pod) (ClickHouseMetrics_ReadonlyReplica)

annotations.description:
A ClickHouse backup job has failed.

Why this matters: once reads and writes both live on the in-cluster server, these backups are the only other copy of the analytics data. A RAID mirror survives a dead disk, not a dropped table or a bad migration.

The schedule is a full backup on Monday and an incremental every other day, each incremental based on its own week's full rather than on the day before it. So a failed **full** also fails that whole week's incrementals, because their base is missing: fix a Monday failure the same day rather than waiting.

Read the job's logs before re-running; the pod is short-lived enough that the log collector often misses it, so `kubectl logs job/<name>` while it still exists is the reliable route.

Likely causes:
- Object storage credentials or bucket policy: the disk reads them from the object-storage Secret at server startup, and an empty key signs a request that comes back as Access Denied rather than as a missing credential
- The in-cluster server being unreachable or read-only
- A full backup missing, when an incremental fails

To run one by hand: kubectl create job ch-backup-manual --from=cronjob/tuist-tuist-clickhouse-backup-full
annotations.summary: ClickHouse backup {{ $labels.job_name }} failed in {{ $labels.cluster }}

model.expr: max by (cluster, job_name) (kube_job_status_failed{job_name=~"tuist-tuist-clickhouse-backup-.*"})

annotations.description:
The two ClickHouse servers no longer have the same schema.

Why this matters, and why it is separate from rows diverging: while ClickHouse Cloud is still the system of record, a column the in-cluster server lacks costs a dropped mirrored write, which is swallowed by design. At the moment that server becomes primary those writes are no longer the mirrored kind and the ingest path breaks outright. This is the condition to clear before a cutover, not after one.

It should not normally happen: `Tuist.Release.migrate` reconciles the in-cluster schema from the source's DDL on every deploy, creating tables it lacks and adding columns, deliberately never dropping or retyping. That reconcile is best-effort so an unreachable server cannot fail a deploy, which is exactly when this fires.

What it will not fix by itself: a column whose type changed, which is named in the migrate job's log and left for a person, since whether the data survives the change is a judgement call.

Where to look: the `tuist-tuist-server-migrate` job's log for `Could not reconcile` or `column type changed`.
annotations.summary: {{ $value }} table(s) or column(s) differ between the two ClickHouse servers in {{ $labels.cluster }}

model.expr: max by (cluster) (tuist_clickhouse_parity_schema_drift)

annotations.description:
Writes that should have reached both ClickHouse servers reached only the system of record.

Why this matters: a mirrored write that fails is logged and dropped on purpose, so that a request never fails or slows because the second server is unhealthy. The trade only holds if the drops are visible, and this is what makes them visible. Each one is a row the in-cluster server will never have unless the backfill is re-run.

A burst in the first seconds after a pod starts is the known shape: the mirror's connection pool is not ready yet. Writes are retried three times before being counted here, so anything reaching this alert has already survived that.

Repair: re-run the backfill with a cutoff later than the drops. It copies only the rows the destination lacks, so it is safe to run again and will not double-count into the materialized views.

Likely causes:
- The in-cluster server is down, read-only, or its disk is full
- Its schema is missing a column, in which case the schema drift alert should also be firing
- Sustained load past the mirror's in-flight bound, which drops rather than queueing without limit
annotations.summary: {{ $value }} mirrored ClickHouse write(s) lost in the last 30m in {{ $labels.cluster }}

model.expr: sum by (cluster) (increase(tuist_clickhouse_shadow_write_count{result=~"error|dropped"}[30m]))

annotations.description:
The ClickHouse data filesystem has been above 70% for 30 minutes.

This fires earlier, and with different advice, than the fleet-wide Bare-Metal Node Disk Usage Watermark at 80%. That one is written for the Kura ring and runner caches, where the answer is another box. Here it is not.

What 70% buys you: on the production box that is roughly 2.3 TB free, and the dataset grows about 0.25 TiB a month, so this is months of warning rather than hours. Treat it as a planning trigger, not an incident.

What to do, roughly in order of how much they give back:

- Retention. Most of the database has no TTL. Note the constraint before reaching for it: about 72% of it is unpartitioned, and a DELETE TTL there rewrites parts through mutations rather than dropping them, so it is expensive and slow. Retention on a table already partitioned by month is cheap; retention on the rest is a repartitioning project.
- Tiering cold parts to object storage with an `s3` disk plus a `cache` disk. This is the intended answer when the box genuinely fills, and it needs the same repartitioning as retention, so plan the two together.
- A bigger box, which is the last resort rather than the first.

Do not react by adding a replica: replicas are full copies, so a second one does not add capacity.

annotations.description:
The hourly parity check found tables whose contents differ between ClickHouse Cloud and the in-cluster server.

What it compares: a two-hour window, not the whole dataset, and it fingerprints each table over row counts, the sums of its numeric columns and its time bounds rather than counts alone. So this is a real difference in recent data, not a merge-timing artefact: the comparison reads through FINAL where the engine collapses rows, and excludes anything written in the last five minutes so a row still in flight cannot look like a lost one.

Repair: re-run the backfill with a cutoff later than the divergence. It copies only the rows the destination lacks, which is also why it is safe to run more than once and will not double-count into the materialized views.

This usually follows something else rather than happening alone, so check whether the mirror-losing-writes or read-only alerts are also firing; those name the cause, and this one names the consequence.

Derived tables are deliberately not counted here. They are recomputed on the destination by its own materialized views rather than copied, so some difference is expected: a Replacing target can keep a different row of a duplicated key, and a base table with a TTL has dropped rows its aggregates still count on the source.
